name: Sri Lanka Portuguese
catalog_citation: Smith, Ian R. 2013. Sri Lanka Portuguese (survey chapter 41). In: Michaelis, S.M., Maurer, P., Haspelmath, M. & Huber, M. (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages / APiCS Online. Leipzig: MPI-EVA. https://apics-online.info/surveys/41
catalog_locator: APiCS Online survey 41, section 4 'Phonology', paragraph on vowels (immediately before Table 1. Vowels)
catalog_quote: Sri Lanka Portuguese retains the oral vowels of Middle Portuguese (except marginal ə), losing contrastive nasalization, but adding a vowel length contrast, as shown in Table 1. ... Only the last underlying long vowel remains long on the surface, the others being shortened. Stress is non-contrastive, falling on the syllable containing the long vowel, or on the initial syllable if the word has no long vowel (e.g. míída ‘measure’ N, midíí ‘measure’ V, mididóór ‘measurer’, jínjiviri ‘ginger’).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding APiCS passage is verbatim in the held at the stated locator (section 4 Phonology, before Table 1). (2) Deciding source: APiCS Online ch. 41 (2013) is a survey chapter, but written by the primary describer and resting on his 1977 Cornell phonology dissertation, which Glottolog lists as the MED (244 pp). That dissertation was not held; it is openly available from MPG's Language Description Heritage (CC-BY) and is now saved with a fetch record at Its section II.3 (pp. 62-100) states the rule explicitly (p. 67: 'stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first vowel of a word having no long vowel'; p. 63 'Stress... is fully predictable'), i.e. exactly our coding: weight-sensitive, unbounded, rightmost CVV else initial, non-contrastive. sources.citation: Seo, Jeong-min & Hak-haeng Jo. 2008. Stress assignment and opacity in Batticaloa Creole Portuguese. Studies in Phonetics, Phonology and Morphology 14(1): 91-105(107). doi:10.17959/sppm.2008.14.1.91 (KCI open full text).
sources.quote: pp. 93-94: 'According to Smith (1977: 67) and Koontz-Garbodean (2000: 1, 5), the stress assignment in BCP is very predictable. That is, stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first vowel of a word if a word has no long vowel underlyingly'; 'the stressed syllable ... changes according to the position of the underlyingly rightmost heavy syllable ... outside of the initial syllable, length is neutralized'; fn 4: 'in BCP, only syllables with long vowels are heavy'. OT-CC reanalysis of Smith's data.

sources.citation: Koontz-Garboden, Andrew J. 2000. Opacity in Batticaloa Creole Portuguese stress assignment: motivation for candidate-to-candidate faithfulness. Ms., Indiana University, Bloomington. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-395. 27 pp.
sources.quote: p. 1: 'According to Smith (1977), stress assignment in Batticaloa Creole Portuguese (BCP) is fully predictable: stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word...'; p. 2: 'it is the rightmost heavy syllable which receives stress; however, in the absence of a heavy syllable, the leftmost light syllable is stressed ... long vowels, which cause a syllable to be heavy, are not permitted outside [the initial syllable on the surface]'; p. 7 fn: 'In BCP, only syllables with long vowels are heavy.' All data from Smith 1977 (OT reanalysis, no new fieldwork).
sources.locator: Abstract p. 1; p. 2; p. 5 (quoting Smith 1977: 67); fn on p. 7

sources.quote: p. 63: 'In Batticaloa Portuguese ... long and short vowels now stand in contrast. All unstressed vowels are short ... all surface long vowels are stressed.
